word_order: SVO | verbs typically appear between a preceding nominal subject and their object/complement in examples like 'mammals were unable to make the journey' and 'People were hitting the panes'.
register: formal written/expository prose (news/encyclopedic style) with some quoted conversational lines and reported speech
discourse_markers: prepositional/temporal/causal adverbials used as clause openers (due to, for over)
extraposition/anticipatory 'it' as a discourse opener (it is estimated)
reporting/quotative verbs that introduce reported clauses or quotations (said, wrote)
clause_boundary_signals: coordinating conjunctions joining independent clauses (and, but)
complementizers and wh-words that begin subordinate clauses and thereby mark the start of a new clause (that, who)
reporting/quotative verbs when they introduce an embedded report or quotation (said, warns)
finite auxiliary/tense morphology signaling completion of a clause (auxiliaries + main verb sequences)
non_boundary_traps: prepositional phrases that look like new clauses but are modifiers (south of Fairbanks; of thousands of barrels)
numerical/measure noun phrases that start a sentence but are single NPs (Eighteen percent of Venezuelans)
participial/gerundial modifiers that resemble verb phrases but attach to a noun or clause (making the giant tortoise...)
relative pronouns or 'where' inside noun phrases/adjuncts that do not end the main clause
unstable_prefix_signals: sentence-initial prepositional/adverbial phrases whose attachment is unresolved until later (for, due to)
subordinating conjunctions or relative introducers that can open either a full clause or a reduced modifier (although, who)
anticipatory/extraposed 'it' constructions whose true complement appears later (it is estimated)
notes_for_prompt_writer: English in this sample is predominantly SVO with frequent embedding (relative clauses, participial modifiers, PPs) that create attachment ambiguities. Coordinating and subordinating conjunctions, relative introducers and reporting verbs reliably start new clauses but some prepositional/measure phrases and participial sequences commonly masquerade as clause boundaries. Quoted speech and extraposition with 'it' are common sites of clause-internal embedding. Auxiliary chains and tense morphology are reliable indicators that a clause is finishing or continuing.
